Updated review for the 1.0 release!!

Core Keeper is a polished, cohesive, and overall amazing experience solo or with friends. From it's early stages Core Keeper has been more than worth it's now 19.99 USD, and continues to promise additional content and a mindful approach to save data.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
Honestly there's so much to cover here so let's take it in sections.

[b]Sound Design[/b]: Beautiful and stylized. The sound design was one of the first things I noticed while playing the game. From the sound of walking on slime, to the sound of stepping on a bug, to the chill tunes that help make this dark world feel like a nice place to call home. Everything about the sound in this game is already pulling me in. 1.0 additions go even further on this, refining more moments of the game to feel even more immersive.

[b]Graphical Design[/b]: The mesh between the way things sound and the way things look is so impressive to me. I love me some crunchy pixel graphics, and the game not only gives me every last crunch I wanted but still serves up pretty and responsive feedback. The consistency between the style of the visual art and the audio is what really won me over though. This game knows what it's style is, and cranks it to 11 in the process. Even after months of playing I still find myself in awe of just how beautiful so many parts of this game are.

[b]Gameplay[/b]: Simple but rewarding. Nothing feels particularly bad in this game to me, and there are almost no things left that I even have feedback for by this point in development! I can chill and feel a constant sense of progress. There is challenge without feeling punished and I love that in this kinda creative-exploration game. It can be a little off-putting at first to figure out what you need to do but that's part of the charm. You're not given instructions. You're dropped in and you just start going and it's very easy to figure out. Your objectives become clear as you play, even though you are never told them.

[b]Potential[/b]: This game has a LOT of potential even after 1.0. I could see myself spending hours making cute bases and grinding my skills up. It will be really interesting to see just how they continue to expand on the ideas already present, because watching the development process up to release has been nothing short of an absolute pleasure. The development team have shown consistent progress and improvements, as well as an open communication that has kept the community trust and engagement there. Not often does an indie team really nail the process, but the Core Keeper team really did knock it out of the park.

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
Let's get into some of the things I didn't love, and we're gonna be really specific here because honestly the game is so great we gotta nitpick to talk about what's bad. Grind grind grind grind. Sometimes a grind is a good thing, but only when you feel a real sense of purpose and value. Some of the skills in the game (I'm looking at you fishing) feel more like a chore because they are slow. The devs have constantly addressed this over time, from making the fishing mini-game more forgiving, to eventually removing it all together. Sadly I find having no fishing mini-game more annoying. I would have preferred improvements to the system that made it easier as you leveled it, give more fish per catch, and level up faster. The removal of this system makes me dread fishing even more because I just stand, click, wait, click. Over... and over... and over...

Crafting stations everywhere. The developers have done a decent job addressing this actually. Although it's still a lot of tables and I wish more of them could mix into a single table with more options in each. What we have seen is that higher tier tables now include all lower tier versions of themselves though, which was not true at launch. Having one Tier 3 table, and one Tier 3 anvil will give you access to Tier 1, 2, AND 3 of each. I'd still like a bit less stations with the combo ones requiring less clicking and searching, but I can at least be okay with the current state!

Let's talk lighting. Obviously the game takes place in dark caves, so we expect it to be, well, dark. It's SO HARD to light up a home though. I don't want to have torches every 4 blocks making the place look kinda ugly just so the place doesn't look dark... I don't think we need torches to be brighter, but we certainly need some fancier lights that work better and look better. I want my home to feel like a home, not just a part of the cave I put a floor on. However, the developers have added some great improvements to lighting since launch. You can put torches on walls now, and you can punch out the "ceiling" allowing natural light without a direct source (though this does have a particle effect too which I don't love for an indoor feel). Not perfect in my opinion, but the lighting has been greatly improved overall.

Lastly I still want a lot more stylized decoration items. I want lots of pretty things to deck my hall out in. I want lots of choices for walls and floors and to have lots of them be able to be recolored. Fancy furniture and lots of options that are just for looks. The game has already done a decent job at adding new decorative items and making existing items like carpets paintable. I just can't say that this is up-to-par with where I want to see the game. This situation has gotten a lot better from the early days but I would still think there is a lot of room for improvement. I want couches, and arm chairs, and counters, and all sorts of little things to allow me to make a solid base.

[h1]Overall[/h1]
The game is a chill experience that gives you a sense of exploration, adventure, and development. It's great to play alone while just vibing, or with friends. This game blew Early Access out of the water, proving the passion of the development team and their dedication to the trust their community put in them. This game was more complete in Early Access then many games are at launch, and now that we are at it's launch it feels so feature rich. What it offers you is well made, beautiful, and already  extremely feature packed, with a promise of more content post 1.0. For the price tag I think it's a great option to spend time with friends.

You can safely ignore @sophistry's "most helpful" review. They've spent a dozen hours and two of Core Keeper's fundamentals have completely sailed over their head:

1. Don't just dig one straight line away from the Core. You'll never reach some of the biomes that way since they're sectioned around the Core. Finding regular ores is trivial if you're in the right biome.

2. You need to surpass an enemy's armour rating to damage it. If you do 50 dmg and dig straight out from the Core like a madman and find an enemy with 100 armour, you can whack at that enemy 1000 times and you'll never kill it. Enemies always do at least 25% dmg to you. This info is in the player stats page if you bother looking.

My review tldr: Terraria with the look and feel of Stardew, as others have said. Early access but like a complete game already--it's good.

To preface this review, I'd like to say that I [i]love[/i] Terraria, I [i]love[/i] Stardew Valley, and I [b]LOVE[/b] that rush that both of those games can make a person feel as they discover new places, make new equipment, or finally kill that one boss. Core Keeper is a fusion of both of those games, and more. It's the experience I wanted as a "casual-but-not-that-casual gamer".

Great game to play alone, even better game to play with friends. This game is what you'd get if you condensed Terraria's caving experience into a single game, think back on when you stumbled upon your first Underground Mushroom Biome or went exploring in the Underground Jungle. It's all those experiences, mixed in with Stardew's combat, but more "focused".

With that said, here's a list of some other notable features that I liked:

[b]Parrying[/b] - I'm currently playing through the game as a melee character, with an axe and shield in hand. With a shield, you can completely negate an enemy's attack by timing a block perfectly (normally, you would negate 70% of the damage, but timing it perfectly would perform a "parry"). Finding this out by myself during a boss fight was really fun, especially with how much I appreciate skill-based mechanics like this. And in Core Keeper with a very lackluster combat system comparable to that in Don't Starve, this is a very welcome addition, making combat vary from just kiting and hitting a boss or mob.

[b]Instruments[/b] - There are instruments in this game! They're all very cute and nice to have, they're also used to solve some puzzles in the game. Overall, they bring personality into the game and could make for some funny moments when playing in a group. I just wish there were more though!

[b]Farming[/b] - Farming in Stardew Valley, but infinitely faster and overall less of a hassle.

[b]Electronics[/b] - Think redstone from Minecraft, but less complicated. You can essentially make a system that mines ore for you while you focus on other stuff in the game. Really cool.

[b]All the little stuff[/b] - There are so much things you can find in this game, don't go into it expecting a speedrun or a challenge run. Just experience it for what it is, dig around, look for some shiny rocks, and maybe you might find some really cool stuff while you're at it.

Absolutely!!! I can't get enough of this game! I turned 60 years old in September and I can play all day if I get the chance! Keep up the great work, I'm trying to get my 22, and 20 year old son's to play with me. Keeping my fingers crossed.   : )

As a 42 year old married man, I honestly wish I could have experienced this game with friends.  No one that I grew up with (or currently interact with) still plays games the way that I do.  Regardless, I enjoyed my time playing Corekeeper.

I logged the majority of my hours during the initial release.  I've never played a game that felt as effortlessly open world as this one.  Building your home(s), exploring new biomes, and even laying out your own railroad network consistently felt fresh and imaginative.

As I dive back in after a number of massive updates, Corekeeper has retained it's original appeal, yet added quality of life updates along with content that has inevitably sucked me back into the persistent grind towards perfection.

Corekeeper will absolutely end up as a top 5 gaming experience in my ever-expanding repertoire.  I'm forever grateful to Pugstorm for the level of happiness they've provided, and I impatiently await the inevitable release of Kyora!

FINAL RATING:  10/10 (first and only game I've given a perfect score!)

Its.... okay. This game lacks a clear identity. It borrows heavily from several other games and implements systems and stylistic choices which reference those games without meaningfully emulating them.
For instance, this game has a similar visual style to terraria, both games also focus heavily on gear based progression, which you primarily obtain through mining, exploration, and by defeating various bosses, both games have NPC's  which are tied to world progression and player built housing, etc.. 
Thats fine, except theres hardly any depth. The exploration in this game lacks most of what made exploration fun in terraria. In terraria you face many challenges to exploration, you start off slow and heavy, with weak mining tools and weapons, to progress you must find a way to delve ever deeper, risking fall damage, powerful enemies and environmental hazards, such as traps, lava, deep water, thorns, boulders and falling sand. In this game, you mine a wall in one direction, fighting the occasional enemy and building the occasional bridge, and thats it.
 Gear progression seems to be entirely linear, you dont really get to branch out into classes, the combat is fairly basic, and the housing mechanics are pretty lackluster.  I think there's only like 5 NPC's, and the services they provide are pretty meaningless.
The game also incorporates some automation mechanics... and I don't really know why..... As long as you dont trash the resources you gain while exploring you usually don't run out of things you need. Gear is pretty cheap on the whole so the automated drilling and conveyor belts like you might find in factorio seemed a bit unnecessary to me. And that seems to be as far as that mechanic goes.Its not like your manufacturing things en mass....
Its also got a lot of other systems thrown in that don't really make a lot of sense to me, like fishing, farming, and ranching, à la stardew valley.  Cart racing, pet raising and starvation. 
Do you see what I mean about not having an identity? Its simultaneously trying to be a top down action exploration adventure game, with automation, farming sim, survival, and casual party game elements. I'm not saying you cant do that but you should focus on making you game's core features really shine before branching out. If you want to create a dense and interesting game world for your players to conquer, maybe hold off on introducing cart racing until theres more than 3 enemies per biome. These sort of party based relaxation side activities are things that exist to entertain people while someone is off fixing gear or preparing for the next boss battle and the other people are hanging out waiting for them, no one is going to say "HEY LETS BOOT UP CORE KEEPER TO RACE CARTS!", so in order for these activities to have purpose you have to make the core game really good, you have to make people want to waste the time waiting for their friend to finish their gear prep, anything else puts the cart before the horse. Terreria's combat is really good, factorio's automation sim is really good, stardew's farming sim is really good, meanwhile everything in core keeper is just okay.

Core keeper, a charming, engaging 2D/3D cleverly rendered pixel art game which plays great on Steam Deck. At its core (no pun intended) there’s a well thought out game system that offers players choices to craft & build, adventure & exploration and combat & loot. There’s in theory near infinite tile generation where equipment evolution is vital to continued exploration.

One of only few constructive feedback for improvement:

1) Poor optimisation; this game currently has issues with fps tanking & micro frame jitters when you are in/around your base (don’t necessarily have to be a large built or base ~ 100x100 tiles). At around 10 hours in; I started to notice this issue such that it became increasingly difficult to focus on gameplay. The issue is well known within Core Keeper community & Discord. I’ve also raised my detailed bug feedback on Steam & Discord you can see here: https://steamcommunity.com/app/1621690/discussions/0/3818543707183995998/

2) the game is very playable solo but generally speaking is a lot more grinding intensive vs. playing with some online friends. This issue becomes more pronounced if you go from playing with friends to playing solo. Mid-late game; there’re in-game tech tree upgrades & equipment you can get that helps to automate certain repetitive jobs like ore mining (at select few locations randomly generated), conveyor belts etc. Even then, you as a player is still required to constantly mostly harvest, run around to maintain chores, inventory management back at base etc. This tired into the first bug if you don’t have multiple satellite bases.

I think a potential way to improve here is perhaps introduce more game automation features for optimised solo play including NPCs you can give tasks to, more intentional placement of ore deposits etc. close to base etc. In current game, late game is likely to become a routine of plant, harvest, inventory management and travel between your resource hubs. This effectively changes your late game into more life/inventory sim management than say adventuring/Action RPG…

Overall a great game that has real depth & characters that I’d highly recommend.

Unfortunately there is no split screen type co-op, but that is understandable imo because otherwise you'd be tied to the same area or the screen would be too small. The upside is this motivated me to smash together a couple of old PCs into a new frankenstein gamish. Core Keeper is not a revolution. It's a game with very tight design following the standards of games like Terraria with the crafting - exploration - boss battle gameplay loop, except it's top  down. Familiar mechanics under a different guise. The charming pixel graphic aesthetic, combat that is simple but fun, a world that has a sense of mystery but is not steeped in complicated lore. 

There is not a wild amount of variety to the non-boss enemies you will be facing. With some exceptions they are reskins of each other with different variations in attack pattern depending on which biome you are in. Biomes and normal exploration can get repetitive, but then that's a sign you should be moving towards the next boss battle, which is how progression is unlocked. 

The boss battles are not astounding, but they deliver on the basic promise of this genre: each one is more difficult, and each one attacks in different ways. As you progress, combat requires preparation, and evasion reflexes become important. There is not a huge variety in gear and builds, so there is just a few different paths to take in terms of playstyle. This to me is a plus since I'm not in a place where I want to spend ages picking between different complex builds, but if you're into more complexity in this regard, I thought you should know. 

Once you've gone past the first major progression barrier, it is only the strength of your pickaxe that limits where you can explore. Systems like, farming, livestock, railways, boats, infinite resource nodes, automated drills, conveyor belts, and eventually portals will spare you a lot of the tedium of resource collection once you get into the midgame. 

Also most bosses have a waypoint teleporter close to them to make it easier to get back in case you die.

This is one of those games I'll go to if I want to chill after a long day and listen to a podcast while I'm mining, farming, fishing and exploring. It's not breaking new ground (no pun intended), but it's a nostalgic, loving embrace from a genre I love, and it feels like coming home.

In terms of quality/function, this game appears to be one of the few games that do what Early Access was actually meant for. As for how fun it is.......I played it for 4+ hours last night, without meaning to.  The night before that, someone asked what was so funny because I had a giant grin on my face and didn't even know it. This game rules.

I had to think about this for awhile, because while I do vastly enjoy this game for a variety of reasons, there is one major aspect that has continued to frustrate, only getting worse as time goes on.

First, let's start with the positives.
   Adventuring and exploring is great, progression is delightful, and there are so many enjoyable easter eggs, and a decent variety of ways to play through the game itself. The coop experience is wonderful as well, and even though not everyone is able to get some of the legendary items due to limited availability in the world, the rest of the available gear is still comparable enough to make this a more minor issue. If you are a fan of Terraria or other similar survival/adventure games, then Core Keeper will likely be right up your alley. 

Now for the one major issue that I have with the game: the leveling system.
   I love leveling systems and talent trees, and while the talent trees in Core Keeper are relatively simple, they are nice. I would certainly love a more in-depth talent tree, or even some of the less-useful talents reworked, but that is not where my main complaint lies. My main complaint lies in the experience system specifically. See, most games follow a general pattern for gaining experience. Do a thing related to your skill, and you gain experience in that skill. The harder the thing, the more experience you gain. For example, slaying a boss would grant you more experience than slaying a minion, or a common mob. Crafting a complex and/or expensive item gives more experience than crafting a torch. Fishing up a tricky fish awards you with more experience than pulling up a sleepy, never-moving fish. Core Keeper follows this principle for [i]some[i] of their skills.
   See, for a lot of the skills in Core Keeper, you simply gain 1 xp every time you do something related to that skill, no matter how difficult or easy it was. Out of the 9 skills available in Core Keeper, 7/9 of them follow this rule. For some of them, such as Cooking, Gardening and running, this seems to work just fine. Maybe not ideal, but fine. For the rest, this rule ranges from annoying, to downright aggravating. 
   On the simply annoying side, we have Fishing. While Fishing, you can either pull up a fish and start the fishing minigame, or you can pull up an item. In either case, you gain 1 xp. It doesn't matter if you pull up an easy fish in the beginning biome, or an epic fish from one of the lategame biomes. It doesn't matter if you pull up a piece of scrap, or if you pull up a piece of rare gear. It is all 1 xp. This leads to the strange conclusion that in order to level up fishing, you [i]don't[i] want to fish up fish. The fishing minigame takes more time than simply fishing up an item, and nets you the same xp, so if you want to level up fishing, it's better to fish up items, not fish! I am not a fishing fanatic, so this mostly is just annoying, but for anyone who really enjoys fishing in various games, I could see this being quite frustrating. (Also, what is the point of the talent that makes you fishing rod casts go further?? I could see this making it easier to fish from fishing shoals, but you can also build a dock easily enough to make this negligible.) 
   For the frustrating, we have Ranged, Melee, and Mining. For all three of these, you get 1 xp each time you hit something. For Ranged and Melee, it's 1 xp for hitting a creature with a ranged or melee weapon, respectively. For Mining, it's when you hit a wall and deal at least 12 damage. Like most games with leveling, the higher the level, the more xp it takes to get to the next level. These xp requirements become egregious at the higher levels, especially if you do not understand the xp mechanic in the game. I spent the entirety of the game with a melee focused build, and even beat a couple of the end game bosses, including the [spoiler]Atlantean Worm[/spoiler]. By this point, I was barely over level 50 (out of 100, for perspective). For further perspective, the xp required to get from level 1-50 is approximately one quarter of the xp needed to get from levels 51-100. I had not touched a single ranged weapon this game, yet I was at end end game and I was barely 1/5 of the way towards 'mastering' melee. 
   It was around this time when I started scouring the wiki, and learned more about the various mechanics of the game, including the xp mechanics for the various skills. Like many others, I love gathering achievements and I wanted to find the most efficient way to get those delicious level 100 achievements. Imagine my disappointment when I realized that the best way to level up Melee was to fight an early game boss with my fists... over and over again. Not exactly exciting gameplay, and most definitely not intuitive for the majority of players. However with over 15 [spoiler]Hive Mothers[/spoiler] slain by my fists, I had made decent progress on Melee, getting to about level 90. They last few levels are truly a slog, taking at least 1 boss fight each to complete. So leveling Melee proved to be viable, even if it was a bit of a slog. Though, at the rate that these last few levels are taking, I'm estimating at least 10-15 more fights before I get level 100 Melee...Ranged is not much better. In fact, you could argue that it is worse, since you have to use a ranged weapon, meaning that you kill enemies in fewer hits, which nets you less xp... and you have to contend with durability.
   The one that I'm dreading the most is Mining. In games like Core Keeper, Terraria, Minecraft, and so on, Mining is a fundamental aspect of the game. You mine [i]constantly[/i], breaking down walls to get to ores, to explore new areas, to build bases, to make travel easier, and so on. I love mining for ores, I love spelunking into the depths and exploring caverns. With over a decade's worth of experience of mining in Minecraft, my love for it still has not diminished. However, the process that will be required to even attempt to bring my Mining up to 100 in Core Keeper... is asinine. If you are playing like a normal player, you don't want to spend forever destroying each individual wall, so you increase your mining damage to destroy each wall in 1-2 hits. If you do this, you would have to destroy over one hundred thousand walls individually to get level 100. You can't even speed up the process by using hammers to destroy 6 walls at a time, because that still only gives you 1 xp, because it is '1 hit'. To help make sure that your world doesn't look like a strip mine, it's better to level up your mining by hitting one wall several times. Except, if your mining damage is too low, you don't deal damage to the wall. If you don't deal at least 12 damage to the wall after it's armor, you don't get any xp at all. You can try trial and error to attempt to find the 'optimal' walls to grind xp, but it's incredibly tedious. Your best way to do this is to once again use the wiki to find the exact stats for each wall, and then use that info to find the best wall to punch over.. and over... and over.... My mining is level 72, but that is just barely 1/4 of the way to level 100. 

   Vitality and Crafting are the only two skills that do not follow this rule, with Vitality giving you xp based off of the max HP of the monster you killed (capped at 1000...), and crafting giving you more xp for the more complicated/valuable items that you craft. I think that Vitality could benefit from having the cap removed and the xp adjusted for later levels, but honestly, it works well enough as is and probably does need any adjustment. Crafting works well enough, so no further notes there.

In Core Keeper, players are dropped into the center of a massive, procedurally generated cavern. From the heart of this cavern, you mine and gather resources: food to keep from starving, ore for armor and tools. You fight enemies and reveal secrets deep underground.

It’s a classic formula that will appeal to fans of base-builder survival sims, and the game sold more than 500,000 units in the first two weeks of Steam early access. I’ve been describing the game to friends as a top-down Terraria, though it has similarities to stalwart entries like Valheim, Don’t Starve, and Minecraft, with a bit of Stardew Valley as well. Core Keeper’s multiplayer (up to eight people), similarly facilitates a lot of collaboration and strategizing. But the game is far from derivative. It weaves tried-and-true survival sim elements into a tight play loop where the game is the grind in a way that feels meditative without being too repetitive.

Core Keeper feels like a dungeon crawler that you’re creating. You gather materials by mining square tiles, and for most of the game, you’re surrounded by walls that conceal explorable areas. The early game is basically just punching through barriers and filling up your pockets. This digging allows you to excavate different regions and grow the map. But the opening belies much more complexity behind the rocky walls. Like in Valheim, regions have big bosses, though it’s possible to play significant parts of the game while avoiding them. Some of these creatures are genuinely terrifying, but Core Keeper’s pixel art style makes the game feel homegrown.

It’s a familiar cadence: use resources to beef up your base, craft items that help you explore further, gear up for the boss fight, make secondary bases, and improve the return routes to key areas. As the paths you’ve created grow more convoluted, you can rely on your map, which you’re able to pull out as an overlay. And while bosses amp up the challenge, the crafting-focused sandbox design is suitable for people who are less interested in hardcore fighting and more interested in base-building. I've played about 100 hours and so far am having blast with my friend.

All of this is bolstered by Core Keeper’s simple skill system. The more you do a particular activity, the more points you bank to spend on related perks. You choose a starting class, which offers bonuses — I decided to be a explorer, which automatically gave me a lantern. I chose this role because the lantern would really help in the early game so I can see father away. The cooking in Core Keeper is also very extensive, and fun to play around with. A certain type of spicy flower grants faster running, for example, and looks a bit like a burrito when cooked. Eating food is also key for filling up your “hunger” bar and staying alive.

This is an exciting amount of depth for a game that feels simple at first blush. Core Keeper does a great job of slowly revealing its crafting system, and the breadth of ways you can build up your base. You largely learn by doing — unlocking additional perks or finding new materials and wondering “What can I do with this?” — which is a rare quality in a genre that can be encumbered by many archaic rules and difficult-to-navigate screens. I also love those types of games, but I appreciate the streamlined simplicity of Core Keeper, which let me hit the ground running.

It all shapes up into a very inviting experience that teases dense design layers down the road. Even in early access, these feel like the raw materials of a multiplayer survival sim that many people will be playing for a while. I can’t wait to see how it keeps growing.

I particularly enjoyed the early game, but once you beat the first 3 bosses, it opens up into a pretty grindy version of itself (and a larger map). It's kind of the next step after Terraria, Stardew Valley, and Minecraft. There are elements of all of these, and homages to many of them; but I really am enjoying the progression much more than all of them. It's smoother, and the ability to keep your hot bar when you die is amazing. 

There are progression elements of two kinds. The first is the Terraria/Minecraft progression in the items you can craft and obtain from bosses or mobs. The second is the addition of character progression, much as in Stardew, the things you do more often, you get better at doing. Having both is a real win, and I love that just playing will get one more powerful. 

The pre-defined characters really do get a good boost with their beginning stats, and use the progression mechanics to differentiate early players. But the more experience you get doing the things you like doing, the more you're rewarded on that path.

The world, though, is amazing, and I've really been enjoying it a lot. It's almost like what would happen if all of Terraria were underground? The various biomes are fascinating, and the gating of ability to each area is pretty solid, but if you are Just That Good, you can just skip into whatever biome you want, and just use skill in place of the extra damage weapons from the other areas will get you.

The bosses are pretty fair on the most part, and with some of the pre-release updates, the tool system has gotten more balanced and the sheer variety of tools, weapons, and armor is really nice. You can play the way you want to and get the kind of equipment that best suits your style of play and still have a pretty clear upgrade path on all of them.

Core Keeper is a weird game. I think the start is fine, you start making your base and exploring your surroundings, nothing out of the ordinary. The game is gorgeous, both in graphics and soundtrack. It's really chill even though I played it on hard. 

My problem with the games comes mainly from its progression. The progression is kind of like an onion; you have layers of different difficulty, the farther from the core the harder, and in each one there's a boss somewhere that you have to defeat to progress. The layers may not follow the same kind of biome in its entirety, and some ores are in specific biomes. All around the map there's big chunks of ore that can only be mined through excavators, and once you have those set up, the fun stopped for me. 

These big ore veins appear to have unlimited ore inside. That, coupled with the fact that items don't despawn when on the floor (or at least it never happened to me) makes it so you don't even need the best excavators nor the mechanical arm to move ore to a furnace, you just wait, collect the ore, put it inside a furnace and wait some more. It ruined the fun completely. 

The most optimal way of playing is to explore in order to find one of these ore veins, place excavators, and then go and explore some more to find more ore veins and fill the with excavators and so on and so on. When you have one vein of each ore, that's it. You won't be needing to go mining ever again, you will not run out of ore. You craft whatever you need, go for a boss and start again. 

I don't find the combat system interesting at all. Your weapon options are fairly limited, and I've found that in general ranged + dashes its just so much better than melee + shield or mele + dashes. You just keep your distance and the enemies die, the same for the bosses. I think the pets are op, as they can't die and deal a lot of damage. Weapons, armor, accesories, I've found most of them uninteresting, not that much variety. 

The map is just too large compared to the interesting stuff in it. I've already found it big enough when going to slay the three first bosses but when that's done and the game tells you to go even further to go and kill some more bosses I lost it. The trips to the outer layers of the map where taking me 30s of just going in a minecart while I look at my phone because nothing interesting is happening between the rides. It's just too big and a big hassle to traverse. 

I stopped exploring and just went from my base to my ore veins, and back to my place to make ingots. Then I would craft the item to put a map pin in a boss, go there and kill it, and repeat. Maybe I'm doing something wrong but man, I tried to find the fun so hard. It's a really chill game and, as I said at the beginning, I had fun while playing it, but after I recognized a lot of stuff that I didn't like were like, the core (no pun intended) of the gameplay, it just demoralized me. 

I think the game's good, but I guess I didn't find where the fun was once I kinda understood how the progression worked. I don't think I wasted my money. Maybe it's more fun with friends.

Its very much Terraria-Lite. If you love Terraria, youll be able to enjoy this game a lot. That being said, spend enough time with it and youll feel like your experience has rung hollow and want for what it didn't give you. Its easier to describe the game in the ways it diverges from the execution or formula of Terraria than by things unique to it.


-Instead of unlocking new unique weapons and facing new unique enemies, creating whole new dynamics to combat and exploration, Core Keeper has you unlock new automation to do what you already do slightly more efficient.
-only as many unique enemies in the entire game as Terraria has in a biome or two. Each Core Keeper biome has 2-3 enemy types, most being reskins.
-Weapons and armor are standard RPG stuff. Theres nothing of interest about them, the way you fight will remain static from start to late game. Most are either useless to use, or pointless to adapt to using. If a high armor build and a dodge chance build wont change how I actually play the game, why bother revamping my gear and stats to this new armor?
-You can farm and decorate like Stardew Valley. It has its charm.
-The bosses aren't mechanically interesting in any way. Probably the most basic RPG stuff it could be.

In hindsight, it missed the mark to be its own game in a lot of ways. The ocean biome is so cool and exciting to build a boat and start exploring, but restricted because there's random ranged enemies that spawn off screen everywhere to keep you from carelessly sailing... you know... having fun... in a way Terraria's side scroller doesn't let you... what a waste.
Frankly, combat is annoying. Instead of exploring, i'm constantly fighting through the same 2 enemies every few feet. I wish this went souls-like and put way fewer, even harder enemies. Maybe that wouldve made combat more interesting and less intrusive to exploring a kinda neat world. But no, its just a chore.

All in all, this game succeeded moderately well in capturing the Terraria appeal with an imaginative world, and successfully incorporated some Stardew Valley and other things into it. It lacks from any inspiration about how to make combat even mildly interesting, and doesn't have the inspiration to really use that infinite top-down open world properly for the player to have some good fun, but it does keep me from replaying Terraria for my 15th run for a time.

Something you can drink to gain immunity to explosives from allies for a few minutes. Core Keeper has a lot of potential, but its mid-to-late game progression feels lacking. The early game is solid—challenging enemies, a mix of overworld and dungeon exploration, and a mining progression system similar to Terraria (copper → iron → etc.), gradually introducing new biomes, enemies, bosses, and expanded gameplay mechanics. The skill point system is a major highlight, making character progression feel meaningful. Plus, base building, farming, and automation are genuinely fun at the start.

Boss fights are actually pretty fun, with some intense moments thanks to their high damage output. However, later in the game, some bosses feel like they go down way too quickly, even though they hit hard. A better balance—maybe giving bosses multiple phases or tweaking their durability—could make these fights feel more rewarding instead of ending too fast.

Unfortunately, the game starts showing its flaws in the mid-game. The procedurally generated world often feels too vast yet empty, with large stretches of land offering little to no rewards. Some dungeons end up being completely pointless due to RNG, making exploration feel frustrating rather than exciting. On top of that, the game’s randomness makes finding specific items and locations—like the Alien Challenge—an absolute grind, sometimes taking hours just to track down something essential for progression. Certain mechanics, like farming and fishing, feel underdeveloped and don’t add much value to the overall experience.

Late-game progression also leans too heavily on grinding, forcing players to revisit the same environments, which start to feel repetitive due to the lack of enemy variety. Magic and summoner playstyles, in particular, seem neglected compared to other aspects of the game.

Honestly, the main reason I stuck around was because I had friends to play with—otherwise, I might’ve dropped it sooner. Playing Core Keeper really made me appreciate just how well-designed Terraria is. That said, I still hope the devs continue expanding the game because it has the foundation for something great.

An important note, this review is based on the multiplayer experience only, I have not played this game in singleplayer.

If your plan is to play this game with friends, you should be aware that the game has a serious issue that makes the multiplayer experience pretty damn awful, unless you have a specific playstyle, or change it to it.

We started 9 people, fun was had exploring and basebuilding alongside eachother and in smaller groups that ventured out into the world, but the farther we got from the starting zone, the more the server performance plummeted, until the game was nigh-on unplayable because of extreme rubberbanding, resulting in players taking a step forward and then bouncing back and forth for a couple of seconds while the server tried to catch up.

We tried all sorts of things to remedy, following tips from reddit and the forums, but nothing helped, so half our group quit the game.

Us that tried to stick it out found out that if you moved around in a group, we could keep the rubberbanding somewhat in check, but this is really not the way any of us wanted to play the game.  Some wanted to explore, some wanted to build, and that wasn't possible at all.

So, all in all, if you want to play this game with friends, you should be aware that in the current version you more or less have to stick together for the game to be playable, and if that is fine for you, theres a fun game in there.

But if you wan't to play with a diverse group of friends, i'd wait for the devs to patch the issue (and, speaking frankly, I don't think that will ever happen as the problem seems to be systemic to the way they designed multiplayer)

What a game! At the the time of this review I have spent about 100 hours in this game (still not done since it is early access) and enjoyed every minute. If you like sandbox games, exploration and base building then this game is definitely for you. I was asked how I would describe it and the best way to do so is "A Terraria like game with the visual style of Stardew Valley". In this game you obviously spend most of your time exploring but you also spend it experimenting. Most items that you do find has more than one purpose and a way to use it. There are multiple weapons, armor and items to use as well as multiple levels of those. There is also basic skill trees that you get experience in by using your character in specific ways; for example if you use a bow then your range combat experience will develop giving you point to allocate within the range combat skill tree. Building in the game is also extremely satisfying and fun, with multiple building material and types that you can use.

I highly recommend this game and will definitely be playing more!

Pro:
1. Beautiful pixel graphics
2. Large builds variety. There are a lot (now even more with the latest patch) items in the game, that you can use to create varied builds for all your needs. They might not all be the meta, but sometimes it feels like you level up too fast to enjoy all the builds you can make at different game stages. Even so, you can level up items so they become viable even in the end game!
3. It has a story!
4. Complex base building. You have farming, sprinkled with automation, fishing, mob farming, cooking, etc. And it looks great! Material blocks give a lot of room for imagination builds. 
5. Few mods elevate the game to top tier survival QOL. There are AAA games that can't get this right. 
6. Control over your game:  you can modify saves, go creative, generate specific map, use same character over multiple game worlds, backup & transfer, etc. And to top it all, you can even activate/deactivate seasonal events, with unique items, whenever you want.
7. Fun with friends. Every new random map seed is a surprise and the game is not punishing if you die, which you will do a lot at first. 
8. The roadmap for the game is ongoing, and the latest patch brought QOL improvements and content.
9. Game is stable, and very little bugs (can't remember if I personally found any that were noticeable). 
10. I liked the achievements :) and the game is kid friendly while not being puerile. 

Con:
1. Randomness: Drop % on certain items, random skills on pets (see points 2). It pushes you to farm bosses and incubate eggs in the tens if not hundreds. Sure, the XP is good, and the resources you get from the farming also, but it gets really frustrating when you need something for a build, and you spent hours to gather/create the boss spawn items, only for the thing you need to not drop.
2. Pet issues: no incubation automation, random chance to find (not farm!) pet eggs. Random skills on hatched pets from a skill pool. This makes getting a good pet very very hard, unless you cheat/use mods. Mods will at least give you faster incubation, but because there is no way to automate the process, you would have to spawn/load into incubator/hatch/crack hundreds of eggs to get the skills you need. It's tedious even if you cheat. So that leaves you in vanilla to be lucky to find a certain egg and be lucky to get the skills you need after waiting for the hatch. Chances/time investment = very low. 
Also, even if there are a lot of pets, most of the skills are overlapping, hurting their utility and flavor. You will mostly use the same ones, provided you got very lucky in getting good skills for them to begin with. 
Sure, this can be solved with trading and joining other ppls games, but it's not how things work in reality. 
3. Some map seeds might not contain unique items, which you won't know from the beginning. Sucks to find out about this later in the game. Some enemies do not respawn, making farming them impossible.
5. Massive frame drops when using items mannequins (also you cannot store rings/weapons on them). Guessing the game sees the fitted mannequins as players. Bottom line, you cannot use displays for all your builds. I got 10 of them in a room, and lost half of fps in my base around that location. No option for 1 button gear swap also. 
6. You cannot stack gear. 
7. Devs are working hard on nerfing (balancing) most of the meta builds that become too popular. I get the intervention, but I never enjoyed this whack-a-mole balancing act. 


Tl/Dr:

I cannot recommend this game enough. It's quaint, great with friends, small in size, looks good, and gives you tens if not, hundreds of hours of content. And if you want diversity, you can generate another world which you can play with the same character, or even better yet, get multiples for multiple builds and specs, and change between them with a simple quit/join game. 
You got bosses, farming, some automation, biomes to explore, cooking, resources and bases to build based on the terrain blocks that you want and find. It really encourages imagination. 
I wish you could farm the pet eggs and compensate for the pet skills RNG with automation and numbers. I wish that at least some pets were more specialized, making getting them a priority (like Ark). They need a rework. Too many of them are useless right now.
And make no mistake, even if my cons are more than my pro's, I consider them mostly small issues and by no means impacting my enjoyment of the game. Buy it!

I Have Decided to Play Every Game I Own in Alphabetical Order and Review Them All (about 700 games) Will I give up? Probably but let's see how far I get.

I broke the alphabetical rule, but I'll go back to it after. My GF and group wanted to try this out-

Game No: #6 of (716)
Game: Core Keeper
Time Played: 53h
Status: Still Playing

First Impressions
Beautiful art style and nostalgic opening menu music. Expecting a mix of Terraria and Minecraft, you're dropped in without a huge tutorial, I love a game that just lets you play.

Smashing slimes and leveling up skills, I heard the level-up "ding" and saw 12 skills including Mining, Combat, Gardening, Fishing, Magic, Summoning, and Explosions. I considered a bomb-making/melee Dungeon Crawler Carl run, but a great summoning book set my path instead.

Playing in a group, we built our base around the central "Core" and four giant statues, digging a moat around our "castle" by hand digging water from a stream (we didn't know about buckets yet).

We found two beetles, built them a house, and added it to our castle. Terrified our new friends would starve, we roamed far looking for worms (turns out pets can't starve; they just stop producing resources). We hit a horrible gribbly, bean-textured infested area full of maggots. We dug up all the terrain to steal it, filling the space back with dirt, then placed it near our beetles.

The gribbly blocks started spreading a maggot plague across our castle. Since the beetles were breeding, I extended the moat and enclosed the gribbly section so the beetles had easy access to the maggot onslaught while our main castle stayed clean.

Exploring further, we hit a massive iron wall. We uncovered the whole circle looking for a door (there wasn't one). I suggested feeding items to the three Core statues to lower it, making that our goal until we found the goats!

It was a beautiful area with golden grass, peaceful music, and frolicking goats. We couldn't abandon them, so we dragged every goat back, stole every blade of golden grass, and recreated their home attached to our castle, safe behind walls and a moat forever.

With that sorted, we hunted Glurch the Abominable Mass. Undergeared from playing with wildlife, we ran around slapping the giant hopping slime, screaming as his gooey trail slowed us down. After much prodding, he exploded into a chest full of loot. we Screamed "WHO'S NEXT?" feeling like we could take on anything 

Next was Ghorm the Devourer, a giant grub bug circling the middle ring. He rumbled past leaving trails of goo, ignoring our pokes. We dug a massive trench to block him, but his legs placed blocks mid-sprint to fix the road like Bob the Gribbler, he could fix it.

Equipping anti-slime gear and slowing swords from Glurch, we glided over the goo like the Mighty Ducks, slamming him. He ignored us until he got MAD, turning around and crushing two of us instantly. My GF was ice-skating and screaming while we begged her to "JUST SURVIVE!" She did. We peppered him, dodged his U-turns, and poked him to death for another massive loot chest.

The final wall boss, Malugaz the Corrupted, was hidden in a dungeon. We had to look it up turns out you combine hoarded gems to summon him. Overconfident, we brought him in. He immediately spewed fire, burning me alive. I portaled back, leaving a Hansel and Gretel trail of torches to navigate the panic. Health potions trivialized his BBQ into a gentle roast, and the loot gave me a burning set that synergized with my summoning. Now I walk around burning everything. It feels awesome.

With all three bosses down, the giant wall lowered into the floor, revealing... what we thought were ducks (dodos).

Naturally, we gathered every duck, stole the biome, made a pond outside our castle, and scooped pond water with a bucket (discovering one bucket pour fills an entire moat ahhh >< ). We built them a deck to play music on, and since they eat bugs, the maggots came in handy again.

Eventually, the goats ate us out of house and home. They cleared so much vegetation we built a massive field, got tired of manual watering, and mined crimson ore for automated sprinklers just to keep them fed.

To speed up travel, we built a railway/tram network across the map, walling off sections to keep enemies out while we enjoyed mining our way through the underground.

With tracks laid, animals fed, and our base running smoothly, we finished the remaining bosses. We lured down an Ice Lightning Bird with a giant egg, crushing it easily since we were so overgeared.

For the ocean boss, we built a soil bridge to his arena. Noticing only four small land patches surrounded by whirlpools, we paved the entire arena in soil, leaving only his spawn spots open. Bypassing the platforming mechanics made the fight a breeze. It's always satisfying using your brain to outsmart boss arenas.

That's where we are now. Sitting back, I realized how long it's been since a game hit like this. It feels nostalgic yet fresh, fun, and engaging. Fantastic co-op experience we'll definitely keep playing.

Gameplay & Mechanics
The core loop centers around mining, exploring biomes, harvesting resources, and leveling 12 skills simply by using them. Build variety is huge. What makes it so fun is the sheer freedom whether hunting bosses, building base structures, automating farms with sprinklers, laying tram lines, or terraforming whole biomes for pets. Frustrations are rare, mostly limited to long travel before rails or keeping up with crops before automation.

Standout Feature
Total sandbox freedom with world manipulation. Digging up entire biomes, moving water with buckets, paving over boss arenas, and relocating wildlife into custom enclosures right next to your base is incredible.

Verdict
An absolute gem of a game in co-op. Hits the perfect nostalgic vibe of Terraria and Minecraft while feeling completely fresh. Even after 50+ hours of base building, boss hunting, and messing with local fauna, there is still so much to do. Easily worth every second.

Great game with bags of content for early access; highly recommended. 


Gameplay is a cross between stardew for crop growing and fishing, Terarria for bosses, and Minecraft I guess (but in a good way) for the ability to collect and place every wall and floor you find. 
The combat is also much better than any of these and actually feels very serviceable, with good enemy tells, weapon variety and even a dodge roll. 

I am currently playing this with my partners in a shared world and the multiplayer is both seamless and intrinsically fun at it's core. 
I thought at about the 12 hour mark we had hit a progression wall with not that much left to do bar an endgame area and boss. Turns out I was very wrong

At that point the world opened up and there were loads of new places to explore, new enemies to fight and new things to craft. 
Speaking of crafting, absolutely everything in the game is either craftable or collectable. Every single item you see on the ground, including the ground itself and even the water can be mined, stored and replaced somewhere else. 
This makes base decoration and design EXTREMELY satisfying. 

Bosses are genuinely pretty tough and require a bit of planning and probably a few deaths to get past. 
The enemies also hit hard, but can be easily avoided if you learn their moveset, so you are rewarded for skilled play. 

Music is utterly wonderful, with really nice compositions that flow from area to area, I cannot stress how nice the sound track is. 
Graphics are also really nice and the water reflections and lighting look gorgeous in certain areas. 


All in all I highly recommend this in its current state at the low price it's currently sitting at. There's loads of content for EA and the devs are continuously adding more. This isn't a game I would advise waiting for full release as it's definitely got replay value and running a new world once the 1.0 lands is something I will probably do. 

Do yourself a favour if you like crafting games with a cozy (but sometimes deadly) vibe and get this game.

I found that this game had a lot of grinding and a slow item progression system, which was fine for the most part. 

However, I had a problem with the gameplay between the third boss and the fourth boss. If the developer doesn't rework this section of the game, I think a lot of players will stop playing after beating the third boss. The issue is that the gameplay between these two bosses is just not as enjoyable as it could be, and it can be frustrating for players who are trying to progress through the game. 

Additionally, I found the character job feature to be largely useless, despite the fact that it grants additional skill points and items at the beginning. This is because it requires five skill points to unlock new abilities, regardless of your character's job. This means that you'll need to grind for skill points in order to unlock new abilities, which can be tedious and time-consuming. One potential solution to this issue is to adjust the skill point requirements based on the character's job. For example, a miner character might require three skill points for the mining skill and four skill points for the running skill, while a cook or gardener character might require six or seven skill points for those skills. This would allow players to specialize in certain areas and make the progression system feel more balanced and fair. If the skill point requirements are the same for every job, you will eventually reach the same level of progression as other players, which can make the game feel less unique and rewarding. It could also enhance the experience of playing with other people, as players could choose different jobs and work together to progress through the game. I would recommend that the developer consider implementing this change in order to improve the overall gameplay experience. 

Despite these issues, the sense of accomplishment that comes with slowly working your way up and unlocking new items may still make the game enjoyable for some players. Keep in mind that this game is still in early access, so there may be additional updates and changes in the future. Overall, if you enjoy games that require a lot of grinding and have a slow item progression system, this game might be worth giving a try.

TL;DR: worth it, buy it, dont expect the world.

Core Keeper really impressed me initially, with me and all my friends being glued to it after the 1.0 update finally came out. It's the first game that really feels like an actual spiritual successor to terraria, rather than just "terraria inspired". I liked the runescape-style levelling system, I liked the way the biomes generated outwards, and I loved the graphics and music. It was fun that things like fishing and gathering were skills as well, and they fed into your combat to incentivize doing them. As a farmer, I helped kill the first boss by tilling all the movement impeding slime it left on the ground, helping my teammates. A lot of fun and unique ideas to a semi-familiar format!

However, during late game I felt that Core Keeper fell off really hard. It's less like the quality of the content dropped, but more that the game had already shown it's hand several hours ago and nothing new was brought forward. The thrill of exploring began to dull, everyone's skill builds began to homogenise, and the problems with combat began to show. Notably, combat is incredibly boring. At the start of the game it makes sense that the skills weapons have are basic and things are just damage number upgrades of eachother, but 25-30 hours in it still felt that way with no improvement to be found. As a melee, my weapon options were "small dagger with high crit chance" and "huge slow weapon with a long range special move" and I chose to take both- everything I found was mostly just a damage increase. I even went on a multiple hour long excursion strip mining a biome to find a super rare sword fragment to make "the ultimate sword", and upon finally getting it, it was more or less just an extremely buffed version of something I already had. Magic seemed a bit more varied, but my friend was complaining to me that ranged was suffering a similar problem. This made me realize that half of the fun of terraria was how many unique pieces of gear there were- it made exploring and getting rare drops feel interesting and rewarding since you never knew what you were going to get. In comparison, Core Keeper reaches a point where going to a new biome doesn't feel impactful or different beyond maybe getting some new unique crafting stations and being able to decorate your house more. Despite all my playtime, I didn't end up beating the game because by the end I found myself just not caring anymore.

But of course, it's always easier to write about the bad things than the good things. And honestly, I'm still giving a positive review to Core Keeper, and I think I got more than my money's worth out of it. I would say if you like terraria and you're tired of playing it for the tenth time, this is probably your best shot. I hope their next project retains my interest more and brings some new wacky weapons and armour to the table, I think the game could really use it.

It's a fun game with a reasonable amount of content and mild grind, overall a 7/10, worth during sale and more enjoyable in multiplayer.

Pros:
1. A moderately wide array of talents and equipment sets that creates different build options.
2. Talent system that is fun to come up with strategy for levelling.

I've played and 'completed' the game once during it's early access back in 2022, the game has improved and added many more contents since but it still feels underwhelming if you compared it to other similar games with similar price tags. The game is designed with simplicity in mind, albeit having a firm gameplay loop that lasts 30~40 hours, the player could only experience very few surprises during each progression phase, and the game felt artificially lengthen after the first 10-20 hours.

The game is in some extent inspired by Terraria and Stardew Valley, yet lacks the variety of former and QoL of Later.
1. The limited rewards for progression and exploration. Most of the weapons in this game are just reskin with slightly better stats. You can literally keep using and upgrading a early-midgame weapon to beat the game because it is the best option. Aside from 3 armor slots, you only get 1 necklace, 2 rings and 1 vanity(side arm) slot. Necklace and Rings mostly provide stats improvement where vanity slots mostly provides unique mechanics. You can obtain dash/teleport vanity item in the early game, and there is almost no reason to give that up for any other choice. The lack of build options are made up by a powerful cooking buff and talent passive system, but it makes looting from exploration and boss fights disappointing.

2. The lack of sense in progression. You swing your pickaxe at the same speed throughout the game and you harvest your crop the same speed throughout the game. Worse, with the ever expanding circular maps, you walk the same speed throughout the entire game unless you keep eating dishes for a 2 minute speed buff. 
The drill is a good upgrade the first time you obtain it, but it is a very rare hidden loot that is easily missed, and it has crap durability. 
Farming is a major element in this game as it provides materials for cooking, potions and passive talent buffs, yet unfortunately the most QoL you can get is a 5x5 sprinkler and a 5x5 seeding shovel. Even in the late game, your best way to harvest is using a drill to harvest each crop one by one. There should at least be a scythe for quicker harvesting.
The best mobility upgrade player would get is an early game dash vanity aside from a pet and food buffs. Minecarts and race cars exist but they are very unfriendly in most unsafe environment and requires infrastructure. Teleportation portals and waypoints exists but requires a 10 minute charge up time after initial setup. it is technically enough for a lite game like this, but still make late game felt slow and repetitive.

3. Lack of actually intelligent automation options. The game interestingly does offer automation options, but they are too primitive and minimalistic. At the very least, automating ore mining/smelting is very easy to achieve. But automating fishing nets and crop farms is going to result in creating chunky conveyor and wire spaghetti, simply because the machine arm (one way hopper) is not smart enough to properly filter items and cannot properly identify if the target container is full. Meanwhile, the crop machine arm is literally garbage. 

4. Class imbalance. Melee gets the best in-class and in-game weapon in early game. Mage and Summoner suffers the lack of mana throughout the entire game, yet performs worse and Melee and Range class. The lack of mana for mage is so severe that it makes early game levelling magic talent unbelievably slow, because you only gain exp each time you deal magic damage, yet your mana recover too slowly without high level talent passives, creating a dead loop unless you willing to grind for weak mana potions. Even in the late-end game, mage deals poor damage even with legendary weapon and requires long wind-up, just to be almost on-par with what melee can do in 1-hit. Worst, mage actually have worse crowd-control than melee and melee has large area piercing damage and/or knockback.
Summoner is also pathetic throughout the game as your minions despawn over time, yet you barely have enough mana to summon max amount of them.

5. [b]The absolute worse part of the game: Explosions[/b]. The absolute worst part of playing mage is the uncontrollable explosions caused by some of its weapons. Not only you will accidentally blow up your infrastructure and base multiple times, you will also quickly fill you inventory with garbage during exploration. 

Suggestions:
1. More mobility options for mid-late game. Maybe an active skill from the titans. Or perhaps something similar to Rod Of Discord.
2. Harvesting Scythe.
3. Smarter machine arm.
4. Mid-late game pipelines that can replace conveyor belt.
5. Filter recipe with effects.
6. Overhaul of certain UI, like crafting station menu, to show more and all options at once, including lower tier items.
7. Fortification of player-built structures.
8. Ability to move while viewing inventory
9. Quick swapping between loadouts using F1-F3.
10. Permanent mana increase. 
11. Actually useful mage staff that has a strong charge attack, instead of a cheap triple-shot copying range weapons. 
12. Wormhole potion that allows for teleporting to other players.

Great game, I have been looking for a game similar to Minecraft and Terraria and I think this game is what I've been looking for. I do find it a little sad that there isn't quite a whole lot to do as in game play and for just casual game play there seems to be only a small amount of things you can do. I do wish there was a game mode that turned hunger off and or even possibly turned off mobs. Your progression depends souly on you and on your ability to explore and fight. I hope that they expand the game and add more to it. I can see many reasons why this game isn't for everyone. It fells addicting playing for the first time; the game has great atmosphere, musics and visuals. The new biomes that you discover and items that you find gets you hooked into the game. However, after playing for a while the game tends to be a bit repetitive and tedious which causes a burn-out from the game, if you are not a big of fan of these types of games. You generally tend to find yourself unable to mine the new biome stones and ores basically, which forces you to grind for the better tools. There is always new biomes so you do this for most of the game. As a result of this the new biomes that you find tend to be less interesting as the game progresses. Progression-vise I find it to be a bit unoptimized as you mostly get jumpscared and one shotted by bosses while exploring (Don't get me wrong its fun :=), also the rewards you get from bosses arent that great generally, The random stuff you get from mobs are far better for some reason. The bosses are also very straightforward generally and they dont last very long.  If you really like grinding for good items, and mining new ores always this is the perfect game. Anyhow, I believe there's a lot that this game lacks in the long term, but I'll guarantee most of you that you're going to find it very enjoyable  for your first couple of hours that's why I strongly recommend giving it a shot.

First of all, let me just say that this is a great game. With that out of the way, let's delve into the Pros and Cons of this pretty large game.

- - - - - Pros - - - - -

1. Lots of biomes and areas to explore that feel quite immersive with headphones on, (Why are you even playing without headphones anyway?)

2. Great with multiplayer, especially when you see all of your buds going out to get resources. It's quite satisfying when they all come back and swarm your base.

3. Awesome music that fits the surroundings, and is definitely one of my favorite aspects of this game. Some of it is so good, (Ahem, insert Forlorn Metroplis music here) that I stopped playing in some biomes just to hear more music.

- - - - - Cons - - - - -

1. The first, big, glaring con, is the inventory management. The latest update did fix this a little, but it is very, VERY annoying to sort out your inventory in the beginning portion of the game. Dirt, stone, grass, decor that you'll never use, these things all immediately fill up your tiny rows of inventory space. Maybe if there were an item similar to the Encumbering stone from Terraria, this might be fixed. 

2. Another con, is actually one of the pros. It has single player capability, but is definitely designed for Multiplayer/Coop, and unfortunately this requires you to have friends. Wow. I can't believe it. Playing with a buddy though is quite enjoyable.

3. Hard mode. Why on earth is this even in the game. Never, I repeat, NEVER enable hard mode on this game. It pretty much just ruins every good aspect of the game and replaces it with a bad one. It makes certain points of progression just painfully grindy, and quite boring after a while. Just please, heed my warning and don't ever touch this difficulty.

4. And another small complaint is the fact that when passive creatures die, they die permanently. I wish I had known this before committing war crimes- Oops! Sorry, my War Thunder gameplay is spilling into my reviews. Anyway though, don't kill animals, just don't.

Overall, the game is great despite my complaints, and I would highly recommend. 8/10, and if they fix my complaints, (Especially the inventory management in the early game) It could easily be a 10/10. I hope they continue updating!

Core Keeper is, in my opinion, one of the best examples of developer communication in recent game history that I have seen. The result of what happens when you have an open-mindset and lay down a versatile product to a broad audience. Of course, with that kind of mindset for game developing, you need a level of joy and fun which these developers have. Even in early-access, the game felt arguably polished. The developers also regularly put new roadmaps in what they wanted to accomplish and head towards, while hearing out the players opinions and suggestions. Now that I'm an A-dult, I haven't checked up as much, but I do know the developers retain a good reputation. 

When I originally played with friends years ago, on the off chance we noticed a bug, we would point it out, and then maybe a week later that bug was removed. In fact, in the patch notes, we noticed the developers found more bugs than we did when we played; and we'd play for several hours. Furthermore, regarding multiplayer, Core Keeper can hold it's own as a single player game if you want to play on your own, but it sure fits nicely as a multiplayer game. Conclusively, I bought this game 3 years ago, and it's truly expanded upon a simple open-world premise to an intricate exploration game that delivers new surprises at different corners; including it's great replay-ability. Highly recommended all the way! 100/10 

P.S. Only thing I would complain about is the medical/health regen doesn't feel adequate or as good as it could be imo, but it could also be a skill issue on my end ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

With minimal defense from your equipment and the fact that dodging makes the minions stop attacking, it becomes nearly impossible to manage. This forced me to switch to easy mode just to progress.

The game still feels slow, with a lot of waiting around for things like plants, smelting, or spawning slimes. The game also overloads you with random drops, requiring constant inventory management, which is tedious due to limited inventory space. Additionally, the lack of variety in equipment makes most exploration feel unrewarding. With the addition of findable class gear, the anvil has become nearly useless since it still only provides equipment for melee or ranged builds. Plus, you still can't craft directly from chests, which adds to the frustration.(You technically can, but only if your workbench is directly next to the chest. Come on.)

On the plus side, you can now customize world generation, making ore hunting easier. TLDR: The game is absolutely beautiful, gameplay feels very Terraria-inspired, but also feels like a letdown the more you play it.

There are lots of interesting systems which just feel way too shallow, like they just really didn't commit. Levelling up skills can be nice, but the skill trees are absurdly simple and some things just take stupid amounts of time to take to max level. Combat classes feel very unbalanced when compared to each other, and once again, take a stupid amount of time to level up if you're not going for an attack speed focused build (you get 1xp per hit, regardless of damage dealt, for all weapons, for all classes). 
Some things in the game are based on exploration, which is nice, but the world is massive, and only bosses can be found using scanners, other structures (such as Arenas, which are needed to summon a boss, for example) are entirely left up to the player's luck, and that just sucks when you are basically being encouraged to find their band of possible locations in the wiki and then strip-mining the circumference of a 1600-block diameter circle to find them. It's just asking for way too much from the player, while explaining and rewarding way too little. 
On the side of explaining way too little, so many systems are confusing, and you have to rely so much on the wiki to understand even basic things such as how to spawn bosses that are essential for game progression. XP gain is not explained, how to spawn NPCs (which are essential to spawn some bosses) is not explained, electricity systems and the absolute importance of stationary drills are not properly explained, the duration/capacity of drillable ore boulders are not explained (I found out they run out after making a 6000+ conveyor belt linking multiple boulders of different ore types back to a single chest in base... And then my first boulders ran out, and I found out all the infrastructure me and my friends had built was for nothing and we'd been better off just syphoning it to a chest right by the boulder and getting it later).

The game has a lot of potential, but it also just really, really feels undercooked in the gameplay side of things. It tried to do a lot, but failed in providing any meat to the many, many mechanics and systems that the game has. The visuals (especially the water and light rendering) are 10/10, some boss fights are very fun, the music is nice, but the game itself is lacking. I wish the best to the devs and I am thankful for the version of the game that we got in the first place, but I also regret to say that I believe this should have been in development for another year for it to even get close to reaching it's true potential.

Overall, the game is solid, but the attempt to implement pseudo-classes—reminiscent of Terraria—has sparked plenty of controversy. It’s not Terraria, yet the game tries to nod to different damage types—magic, ranged, melee, and summoned-creature damage—so you could read it as a class system. Still, it’s hard to call them true classes: in Terraria, you feel capable at every progression stage, knowing you can clear content with any single path and that multiclassing isn’t just unnecessary, it’s often detrimental. In Core Keeper, by contrast, multiclassing seems essential to progress; without it, the game feels practically impossible after a while.
The main issue is that the balance doesn’t seem tuned for a specific class. Take the warrior: melee works against only a limited set of bosses up close. Slime bosses and Omoroth, however, overwhelm you with constant swarms, making close-quarters combat infeasible. You simply can’t reach them. The viable option appears to be ranged combat with a bow or crossbow. Other weapons are sparse, and their usefulness feels marginal because you must find them first, and even then they don’t match the value of a well-crafted bow.
Another odd design choice involves the mage. In a game where mage is a viable option, not providing mana potions or any mana restoration feels very strange. Waiting for mana to recharge while the boss heals itself—especially against Omoroth with its tentacles—renders mage play effectively untenable. You must damage the boss while contending with its heals, which makes it nearly impossible to land meaningful DPS.
There’s also a summoner path, reminiscent of Terraria 1.3: you summon some creatures, then use any other weapon you like. Yet the summons aren’t especially effective, since they don’t hit as hard as weapons built for a specific style. There are only six summoning weapons, and the fifth one—the jellyfish set—feels useless: to get any action from them you have to dance around the boss, often dying in a single hit. So the game doesn’t feel tailored to any particular class, aside from a viable ranged playstyle. This raises the question: why even have armor for other classes? It seems like diversity in name only; in practice, you can’t play them properly. It’s not about skill alone, but about the overall tuning and balance feeling off.
In my view, ranged combat is the most comfortable path. Other styles feel constrained. Even normal enemies—aside from a few troublemakers like that crab in the sunken sea—pose real challenges. In short, the game isn’t clearly aligned with a single class, except for long-range play, which casts doubt on the whole multiclass concept and the intended diversity of builds.

[b]Core Keeper is a crafting/building game about expansive exploration, in a beautiful but unfamiliar underground world.[/b]

[h3]What you'll want to know:[/h3]
[list]The [b]core gameplay mechanics are presented to the player within the first 30 minutes, and it rarely ever deviates from them[/b]. The variety comes from finding more items, biomes, and bosses as you push outwards.
[b]If you don't enjoy the gameplay during the first hour, you won't later.[/b][/list]
[list]It's great with friends, but it plays completely fine solo.[/list]
[list][b]There's a lot of exploration, but you need to lean heavily on the progression mechanics in the game.[/b][/list]
[list]The combat in the game is very fast. There are times where you get killed within a few seconds. You have to learn to slow down and use mechanics like cooking and armour to mitigate this.[/list]


[h3]Things I loved:[/h3]
[list]The music and graphics are truly works of art.[/list]
[list]The mechanics are uncomplicated, intuitive and polished[/list]
[list]Crafting using nearby containers, and a single button to quick stack.[/list]
[list]An abundance of items. You'll need lots of chests.[/list]
[list]Numerous viable approaches to movement and combat[/list]

[h3]Things I liked:[/h3]
[list]Chill time at base doesn't feel wasted. There's always something you can do or build between ventures.[/list]

[h3]Things I disliked:[/h3]
[list]Pacing slows down dramatically during the second act.[/list]
[list]The game ends pretty anticlimactically.[/list]
[list]Ctrl+scroll wheel to swap inventory layers is neat but becomes overwhelming.[/list]
[list]Huge amount of [b]inter-biome[/b] variety, but not a lot of [i]intra-biome[/i] variety[/list]
[list]Thankfully not a lot of resource grinding, but you are expected to have collected some obscure items.[/list]
[list]hard mode doesn't add as much in-game reward as it suggests.[/list]

[h3]Things I hated:[/h3]
[list]Font is egregious. I honestly gave up on cooking because it's so hard to read the font.[/list]
